item.title: x86 PUSH Operation: Does Immediate Size Determine Stack Push Size
item.description:
“x86 PUSH Operation: Does Immediate Size Determine Stack Push Size”

A frequent point of confusion in x86 assembly programming revolves around the PUSH instruction: Does the numerical value provided to PUSH dictate how many bytes are written to the stack, or is it strictly determined by the instruction’s operand size context?

The direct answer is that the size of the immediate value that fits within an imm8 (immediate 8-bit) encoding does not dictate the operand size for the PUSH operation. The stack pointer (ESP/RSP) is decremented by the established operand-size for that specific instruction execution mode, irrespective of how small the immediate value is.

“Differentiating Register and Memory Addressing in Assembly: Brackets Explained”

In low-level programming, precise control over data movement between registers and memory is paramount. A common point of contention arises when using the MOV instruction: what is the functional difference when an operand is specified directly versus when it is enclosed in square brackets, indicating memory dereferencing?

item.title: Why is the x86 LOOP instruction slow on modern CPUs
item.description:
“Why is the x86 LOOP instruction slow on modern CPUs”

The LOOP instruction in x86 assembly has a peculiar reputation for being significantly slower on modern processors compared to its earlier counterparts. While on processors like the 8088 and 80286 it was often faster than a DEC CX followed by a JNZ, its performance on later architectures, especially those with advanced pipelining and out-of-order execution, has noticeably degraded. What architectural shifts and design decisions led to this performance disparity?
